newsitem.title: USA: FORECAST-US Dec jobs eyed for wages, manufacturing.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-US Dec jobs eyed for wages, manufacturing.

text.p: Analysts expressed concern on Wednesday that December's U.S. nonfarm payrolls report may signal further strength and wage pressures in the manufacturing sector.

The payrolls report, to be released by the Labor Department at 0830 EST/1330 GMT on Friday, follows last week's report by the National Association of Purchasing Management suggesting a rebounding factory sector.
A Reuters poll showed that, on average, December payrolls are expected to increase by 192,000 after some 118,000 jobs were created in November.
Analysts surveyed by Reuters also look for a slight drop in the unemployment rate to 5.3 percent, from 5.4 percent in the last survey.

In addition to the overall number, many components of the report are closely examined for underlying trends. Average hourly earnings are seen rising 0.2 percent in December, down from November's heady 0.8 percent gain. The average workweek is expected to remain steady at 34.5 hours, the Reuters poll showed.
"We think it's going to be a big gain with the biggest gains in the retail sector," Robert Brusca, chief economist at Nikko Securities Co. International, said of the headline number.
He attributed some of the gains to a late Thanksgiving, which led to a belated compilation of holiday season hirings that will be reflected in the December number - a factor widely cited.
The 30-year Treasury bond was narrowly range-bound much of this week in anticipation of the payrolls report with prices falling enough to drive yields near two-month highs.

A mixed bag of recent economic data has suggested to many analysts that fourth quarter economic growth was stronger than expected and that the strengthening trend could spill over into the first half of 1997.

"I've got to confess I have my fingers crossed on this. The last National Association of Purchasing Management's report suggested a strengthening economy in November and that could lead to upward pressures on prices," said Hugh Johnson, chief economist at First Albany Corp.

Johnson said he will closely watch manufacturing payrolls for any surprises on the upside because he feels strong hourly earnings could upset the bond market even if the headline number is benign. Stronger wage earnings often ignite inflation leading to higher interest rates, which erode the value of fixed-income securities.
Despite his reservations, Johnson looked for job growth to be below the concensus rate and come in at 140,000 for the month.
Nikko's Brusca also said there is growing evidence the factory sector is picking up even though the nondurables sector has shown losses in eight of the past nine months.
"The losses have become progressively smaller and the pickup may set a trend that becomes a theme in 1997 - a rebounding manufacturing sector," Brusca said.
With inventories still lean, this could force upward pressure on wages and shake the Federal Reserve out of its mostly inactive 1996 mode, Brusca said.

Analysts also noted the Federal Reserve's policy-making arm meets next on February 4 and 5 and could vote to tighten monetary policy should they view increased production and tight labor markets as inflation threats.
However, the consensus view was that such a move -- if one occurs -- would not happen until the Fed's March meeting.

William Sullivan, director of fixed-income research at Dean Witter Reynolds, said he expected to see continued gains in the health care and government sectors. He too cautioned that pronounced rises in average weekly earnings could trip up the bond market.
